item.title: Kuaizhou targets 2027 maiden flight and first-stage recovery of reusable rocket, unveils development roadmap
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 19:39:00
Kuaizhou rocket model Photo: VCG China's space sector has seen another development in the development of a new reusable launch vehicle, with Wuhan-based Kuaizhou Aerospace targeting 2027 for the maiden orbital flight and first-stage recovery of its Kuaizhou-6 liquid-propellant rocket, which is designed to carry a payload of about 20 tons. The company also plans to conduct at least 50 launches over the next three years using its Kuaizhou-1A and Kuaizhou-11 rockets, the Global Times learned from Kuaizhou Aerospace on Tuesday. According to a press release by the firm, Kuaizhou will accelerate development of its Kuaizhou-6 reusable liquid-propellant rocket, targeting its maiden orbital flight and first-stage recovery in 2027. The rocket is designed to have a payload capacity of about 20 tons. By the middle of the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the company plans to upgrade the rocket with a 140-ton-class liquid-propellant engine and put it into large-scale commercial service, further increasing its payload capacity and advancing the engineering application of reusable launch technology. The company also plans to develop lower-cost medium-lift launch vehicles. Building on its existing technologies and production capacity, it will adopt a standardized, modular and flexible approach to developing the Kuaizhou-12 solid-liquid hybrid rocket. The rocket, with a payload capacity of about 10 tons, is scheduled to make its maiden flight and enter the market in 2027, with a targeted launch cost of no more than 20,000 yuan ($2,800) per kilogram. Kuaizhou also outlined a three-stage roadmap for its liquid-propellant engine program. In 2027, it aims to complete a cumulative 15,000 seconds of hot-fire testing for its 80-ton-class liquid oxygen-methane engine and deliver the engine for operational use, while completing design-validation hot-fire tests of a 140-ton-class engine. Before 2030, the company plans to complete design-validation hot-fire tests of a 200- to 300-ton-class liquid oxygen-methane engine. Meanwhile, Kuaizhou plans to conduct more than 50 launches over the next three years using its Kuaizhou-1A and Kuaizhou-11 carrier rockets, aiming to establish routine, high-frequency launch operations. The company said the effort would help consolidate its rapid space-response capabilities and support national emergency needs. To further expand its ambitions, Kuaizhou plans to strengthen its research, testing and final assembly facilities at its Wuhan headquarters, while further developing its liquid-propulsion research and development center in Beijing. The company also plans to expand its testing capabilities for 300-ton-class liquid-propellant engines and establish testing and launch capabilities in Jiuquan and Wenchang, aiming to achieve independent control over the entire chain of research, development, production and testing.

item.title: Book of Xi's discourses on poverty reduction, alleviation published
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 19:29:00
CHINA / POLITICS Book of Xi's discourses on poverty reduction, alleviation published By Xinhua Published: Nov 10, 2026 07:29 PM
A compilation of discourses by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, on poverty reduction and alleviation has been published by the Central Party Literature Press and released nationwide. Compiled by the Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee, the book brings together 55 important articles by Xi on poverty reduction and alleviation. Some of these works are made public for the first time. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the CPC Central Committee with Xi at its core has placed poverty alleviation high on its governance agenda and regarded it as the bottom line task in building a moderately prosperous society in all respects. China has won a complete victory in the fight against poverty and accomplished the arduous task of eliminating absolute poverty, creating a miracle in the human history of poverty reduction. In the process, the country has blazed a poverty reduction path and formed an anti-poverty theory with Chinese characteristics. Xi's discourses on poverty reduction and alleviation represent an important theoretical achievement in China's poverty alleviation efforts and the latest achievement in adapting Marxist anti-poverty theory to the Chinese context. These discourses provide important guidance for consolidating and expanding the achievements in poverty alleviation and advancing rural revitalization across the board, promoting modernization that delivers common prosperity for all, and building a better world free from poverty and featuring shared prosperity.

item.title: Construction begins on highest pumped-storage power station in Northwest China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 18:47:00
Delingha pumped-storage hydropower station Photo: Screenshot from web China has started construction of the Delingha pumped-storage hydropower station in Northwest China's Qinghai Province - the highest-altitude pumped-storage power station in Northwest China, according to the CCTV News, citing the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council (SASAC). Located in Xuji township, the project has a total installed capacity of 600 megawatts. The normal water storage level of its upper reservoir sits at an altitude of 4,008 meters, the CCTV News report said. With a total investment of 5.23 billion yuan ($783 million), the station will mainly comprise upper and lower reservoirs, a water conveyance system and an underground powerhouse. It is designed to generate 1.2 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity annually and consume 1.6 billion kWh for pumping each year, with full operation expected in 2034. A pumped-storage plant is a green energy storage facility that supports flexible grid regulation. During off-peak hours, surplus power is used to pump water from the lower reservoir to the upper reservoir, storing electricity as gravitational potential energy; during peak demand, the stored water is released to generate power. It performs key grid functions including peak shaving, frequency and phase regulation, and emergency reserve. Listed as a key project under the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-25) in the National Energy Administration's Medium- and Long-Term Development Plan for Pumped Storage (2021-35), the Delingha station will shore up grid regulation for the city's 10-gigawatt clean-energy base and fill the gap in large-capacity energy storage in the region. Sun Chuanwang, a professor at the School of Economics at Xiamen University, told the Global Times on Tuesday that the pumped-storage hydropower station, which is close to the massive clean energy base in the city, will greatly facilitate efforts in conserving and utilizing the clean energy. With an altitude of 4,300 meters, the Daofu pumped-storage power station in Daofu County, Southwest China's Sichuan Province, is set to be the world's highest-altitude pumped-storage power station, according to the Xinhua News Agency. Qinghai's Delingha is home to extensive new-energy infrastructure, including solar power generation installations, green hydrogen production facilities, heat-absorbing towers and energy storage facilities. By 2026, Delingha had a total installed clean energy capacity of 6.05 million kW, with another 950,000 kW under construction, according to city authorities. The city is striving to see its clean energy installed capacity breaking 14 million kW by 2030.

item.title: Lithuania reportedly seeks Taiwan island office renaming; Chinese expert says respect for China's core interests key to mending ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 15:13:00
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda talks to media prior the start of an EU Summit in the Europa building on June 18, 2026 in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: VCG Words alone will not mend Lithuania's fractured ties with China, a Chinese expert warned, as reports emerged that Vilnius had pressed so-called "Taiwan's Representative Office" to change its name and Lithuania's president called for normalizing diplomatic relations with Beijing. The real test, the expert said, is whether Lithuania is prepared to move beyond what he described as political opportunism and take concrete steps to respect China's core interests. Representatives of the Lithuanian Foreign Ministry presented the "Taiwanese Representative Office" with an unofficial document setting out demands, including that Taiwan change the name of its office in Vilnius, the delfi.lt news website reports. According to the website, the document was presented to the office at a meeting on September 24 attended by Deputy Foreign Minister Vidmantas Verbickas and diplomat Ričardas Šlepavičius. The document stated that the current name of the "Taiwanese Representative Office" was hindering the development of economic ties between the two sides and urged Taiwan to change it by October 1, according to delfi.lt news. Speaking with reporters, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said he had been briefed on the Lithuanian Foreign Ministry's talks with the "Taiwanese Representative Office" in Vilnius about a possible change to its name. "All matters are coordinated with me. We no longer live under the previous government, when the foreign minister [Gabrielis Landsbergis] could open a representative office simply by exchanging letters with another state, without consulting other institutions. Such nonsense no longer happens in Lithuania," Nausėda told reporters, according to Lithuanian broadcaster LRT. According to Nausėda, relations with Beijing are currently "practically zero," making the restoration of diplomatic representation the first priority, per LRT. He stressed that Lithuania wanted to normalize relations with China while maintaining good ties with the island of Taiwan. The Lithuanian government, in disregard of the Chinese side's strong objection and repeated dissuasion, approved the establishment of the so-called "Taiwanese Representative Office" in Lithuania by Taiwan authorities in August 2021. Under the one-China principle, any exchanges with China's Taiwan should be civil and non-official. By allowing the establishment of a "representative office" under the name of "Taiwanese," Vilnius has apparently reneged on the political commitments it made in the communiqué on the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Lithuania. Since then, China has adopted a slew of legitimate, reasonable and lawful countermeasures including a diplomatic downgrade between China and Lithuania. No Chinese diplomats have remained in Lithuania since May last year, according to Lithuanian media reports. Lithuania's recent signals of a willingness to improve ties with China stem largely from the realization that its previous approach to the Taiwan question has come at a cost, Jian Junbo, director of the Center for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University, told the Global Times. Jian said despite its repeated overtures, Vilnius has yet to take concrete steps toward mending relations, reflecting what the expert described as an opportunistic approach to Beijing — seeking to maintain ties with both sides without making a clear choice. The prospect of a genuine rapprochement, Jian said, ultimately hinges on whether Lithuania is prepared to respect China's core interests through concrete actions, recognize the Taiwan question as a red line for Beijing and uphold the one-China principle. In June, Nauseda told Bloomberg TV in an interview that he expected to see the first results of the country's diplomatic outreach to China within the next six months. "We'd like to normalize the political relations because those relations have been broken for a few years," Nauseda said. "We are in the process, and I hope that we will see the first results in the next six months." The onus is now on Lithuania, rather than China, to advance the normalization of bilateral relations, Jian said. While Vilnius has signaled a willingness to improve ties, meaningful progress will depend on whether it demonstrates genuine sincerity through concrete actions on the Taiwan question. Such steps could help create the political conditions needed to resolve existing differences and pave the way for a restoration of normal relations, he added. In June, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that China had repeatedly made its position clear on China-Lithuania relations. The crux of the current difficulties was that the Lithuanian side had violated the one-China principle and gone back on its political commitment made in the joint communiqué on the establishment of diplomatic relations. China remains open as always to communication, Guo said, who expressed hope that the Lithuanian side would act promptly and decisively to correct past mistakes and return to the right track of adhering to the one-China principle so as to create conditions for the normalization of relations with China.

item.title: GT Voice: Japan can't diversify its way out of losing Chinese tourists
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 00:15:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT With Chinese arrivals falling sharply, Japan's tourism industry is having to look for new sources of visitors. Nikkei Asia reported on Sunday that Japan was stepping up efforts to attract Indian visitors, with hotels and travel agencies expanding services tailored to them, including meal options and activities. India is indeed an expanding source of visitors for Japan. According to the Japan National Tourism Organization, arrivals from India rose 19 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026. Some other markets also posted strong growth. Yet Japan's broader tourism figures tell a less encouraging story: total international arrivals fell 2.9 percent over the same period. The decline in Chinese arrivals shows the limits of diversification. In the first nine months of 2026, the number of visitors from the Chinese mainland fell 55.5 percent year-on-year, a drop of more than 4 million. That is a substantial loss for a country that received just 30.7 million international visitors over the same period. It seems that Japan's sustained efforts to diversify its visitor base have so far failed to fill the gap left by Chinese tourists. Diversifying its visitor base makes sense for Japan, but that does not mean it can afford to let Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's erroneous remarks on Taiwan alienate Chinese tourists, given China's longstanding importance as a source market. Japan's Jiji Press reported in March that as Chinese arrivals declined amid strained relations, the Japanese government planned to focus on attracting more visitors from Europe, the US, Australia and other regions. If the strategy is judged by whether it can significantly boost Japan's overall inbound visitor numbers, it has failed so far. Japan's inbound visitor numbers will need to grow substantially, from about 42.7 million in 2025 to 60 million by 2030, to meet the government's target. Reaching that goal will be considerably more difficult if Chinese tourists remain a missing piece of Japan's tourism growth picture. Japan's inbound visitor numbers grew by 15.8 percent in 2025, with Asia accounting for part of that growth. As Asian economies continue to expand, more people in the region have the means and the appetite to travel abroad, creating new opportunities for destinations such as Japan. This trend was reflected in the first nine months of 2026, when arrivals from South Korea, India, Malaysia and Indonesia all rose by double digits. Yet this growing demand failed to translate into an increase in Japan's overall visitor numbers. Japan was well-placed to benefit from Asia's expanding appetite for overseas travel, but the steep decline in Chinese arrivals has left much of that potential unrealized. Chinese mainland residents made 148.36 million outbound tourist trips in 2025, up 20.8 percent year-on-year. Chinese outbound tourism is becoming an increasingly important source of visitors for destinations throughout Asia. Japan, with its own ambitions for tourism growth, can ill afford to turn its back on a market of this scale. Restoring Chinese tourists' confidence in visiting Japan will take more than promotional campaigns. Japan must address the damage caused by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's erroneous remarks on Taiwan, which lie at the root of the current situation in China-Japan relations. Consider this: when choosing where to spend their holidays, how many Chinese tourists would willingly travel to a destination where they feel their national sentiments have been deeply hurt? The answer is unlikely to be many. Those in Japan who expect visitor diversification to drive overall tourism growth and help the country reach its target of 60 million international arrivals by 2030 may be disappointed if they believe the Chinese market can simply be replaced. Diversification can broaden Japan's visitor base, but it cannot make the loss of such a large market any less consequential. Rebuilding Chinese tourists' confidence and regaining their goodwill are not optional extras. They are steps Japan's tourism industry can hardly afford to avoid if the country is serious about making meaningful progress toward its 2030 tourism target.

item.title: Worried about being 'snubbed' at APEC meeting? Tokyo has a guilty conscience: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-10 00:01:00
Illustration: Liu Rui/GT If today's Japan were genuinely contributing to regional prosperity and had earned the recognition of its neighbors, would it really need to be so suspicious? Tokyo's unease, in fact, shows Japan knows full well what role it is playing today. Japanese media have recently cited unnamed sources as saying that the Japanese government is seeking assurances from China that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will not be "snubbed" by the Chinese side at the upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting. According to these reports, Tokyo is concerned that any "unusual plan" or public criticism of Japan by China could be seen as an attempt to "embarrass" Takaichi, in which case Japan would lodge a protest. It is obvious that these "unnamed sources " were not speaking mainly to the Chinese side when they chose to make such remarks to the media. By sending out signals through the press ahead of the APEC meeting that it is seeking assurances, Tokyo appears to have at least two objectives. First, it wants to give itself a convenient excuse in advance and satisfy hardline voters at home: If Japan is snubbed on the international stage, the blame should lie with China, not with the consequences of the Takaichi administration's own policies. Second, it attempts to shape the narrative for the international community in advance, indirectly framing any deterioration in relations as a sign of China's alleged failure to act with the magnanimity expected of a major power. This is a familiar tactic from Japan. At the same time, the extensive attention Japanese media have devoted in recent days to the question of how Takaichi might be treated at the upcoming meeting is telling in its own right. Why has an event that should be focused on cooperation across the Asia-Pacific come to be viewed by some in Japan as a minefield of potential snubs and slights? The answer likely lies in Japan's own words and actions over the past period. Since taking office, Takaichi has repeatedly sought to blur Japan's responsibility for its history of aggression, accelerated efforts to push beyond the principle of its "exclusively defense-oriented policy," and repeatedly crossed lines on the Taiwan question by invoking the notion of a "Taiwan contingency." These moves have seriously undermined the political foundations of China-Japan relations. In truth, Tokyo's current anxiety stems from its fear that its own actions may eventually carry consequences in a multilateral diplomatic setting. This is a textbook case of a government with a guilty conscience. Japan is pushing constitutional revision, expanding its military capabilities and whitewashing its history of aggression at home, while worrying that it might be "snubbed" at multilateral events abroad. This concern itself points to a fundamental mismatch between its policies and its expectations. In reality, a country's standing in regional affairs ultimately depends on what it can contribute to common development and whether it can convince its neighbors that its commitments are credible. Japan has long been an important participant in Asia-Pacific trade and investment, and a beneficiary of the postwar international order. If today's Japan were genuinely contributing to regional prosperity and had earned the recognition of its neighbors, would it really need to be so suspicious? Tokyo's unease, in fact, shows Japan knows full well what role it is playing today. In fact, for Japan, what truly earns it respect on the international stage is not any "guarantee" demanded in advance, but its own concrete actions. APEC focuses on development and cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region. Its core agenda has always centered on trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, supply chain resilience, the digital economy, green transformation and other issues. Reducing the core concerns of APEC participants to questions such as "Will I be treated differently?" or "Will I end up on the menu?" fundamentally narrows and distorts the nature of APEC. It also reflects Japan's distorted view of international relations today. Such thinking not only underestimates the composure and resolve of other members but also exposes Japan's anxiety about its own position. In the long term, this distorted worldview and set of values will further weaken Japan's position in regional cooperation. Asia-Pacific economic integration is entering a new phase driven by the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the vision of a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, with participating economies placing greater emphasis on regulatory consistency and policy continuity. When a country's leader devotes substantial political energy to breaking through established constraints and stirring up sensitive issues, other members will naturally reassess the political risks of deepening cooperation with that country. APEC is not a mechanism for punishment, but neither is it obligated to cover up any country's embarrassing conduct. If Japan continues to turn its domestic political needs into external provocations and then blames others for the resulting diplomatic setbacks, it will only further erode its credibility in regional affairs. What Japan should truly be concerned about is not the opportunity for a handshake or the seating arrangement for a group photo at a particular meeting, but how its misguided policies are steadily eroding the trust of neighboring countries, ultimately leaving it with increasingly limited diplomatic options. On China-Japan relations, China's position has remained consistent: The two sides must return to the spirit of the agreements reached in 1972. Rather than trapping itself within constraints of its own making, Japan should seriously reflect on its understanding of history, policies toward China and regional strategy, stop taking actions that undermine regional peace and stability or harm other countries' core interests, and demonstrate genuine sincerity in pursuing cooperation. It should stop pretending not to understand the situation while knowingly engaging in disruptive behavior and simultaneously demanding preferential treatment.

item.title: New BCI and neuromodulation technologies help military pilots combat mental fatigue, enhance performance
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 21:23:00
Photo: Screenshot from CCTV From brain-computer interfaces (BCI) and neuromodulation to advanced flight training technologies, an aerospace medicine summit hosted by the Air Force Medical University over the weekend in Xi’an, Northwest China’s Shaanxi Province, showcased the latest advances in aerospace medicine, flight training, and aeromedical rescue, China Central Television (CCTV) reported on Sunday. More than 1,000 experts and scholars from across China, including the military, gathered to discuss key challenges and cutting-edge developments with the aim of advancing high-quality scientific and technological innovation in aerospace medicine, according to CCTV. At this year's forum, a key topic of discussion was the application of BCI and neuromodulation technologies to strengthen aircrew members' physical and psychological resilience and sustained combat effectiveness under high-intensity missions. Experts discussed ways to protect aircrew from extreme physical and psychological stress, improve personnel selection and training, and leverage digital intelligence to enhance aviation capabilities. Yang Liu of the Air Force Medical University said pilots undergo training using breathing exercises and biofeedback before missions. Between missions or afterward, brief and safe transcranial microcurrent stimulation can be used to modulate brain regions associated with cognitive functions, helping pilots quickly alleviate mental fatigue. In addition, efficient personnel selection and training, as well as the integration of digital intelligence technologies, were among the key topics discussed at the forum. The forum also highlighted advanced flight training technologies, including a spatial disorientation simulator that recreates illusions encountered during night flights and when flying through clouds. The immersive system helps pilots maintain spatial awareness and better control their aircraft, enhancing flight safety. For example, when some pilots conduct training exercises in the deserts of northwest China, both the night sky and the ground can be completely dark due to the absence of artificial lighting. Pilots may experience spatial disorientation, mistaking the ground for the sky and vice versa, posing serious safety risks. Specialized ground-based simulators recreate realistic flying environments to help pilots recognize and respond to such illusions effectively. The forum also featured innovations in cognitive computing and non-invasive BCI aimed at enhancing aircrew operational capabilities, including an attention assessment and training system. The system uses real-time eye-tracking and physiological data to monitor pilots' attention distribution, cognitive workload and stress levels in complex environments. Models based on expert knowledge automatically score performance, helping trainees identify weaknesses and undertake targeted training, driving a shift in cognitive skills training from experience-based instruction to data-driven training supported by digital technologies. In addition, emerging forms of information-driven, intelligent and unmanned warfare are changing combat injury patterns and casualty evacuation conditions, creating new challenges for aeromedical rescue and rapid treatment. Wang Jianqi of the Air Force Medical University said researchers had developed the Chinese military's first casualty-search drone. They had also made advances in using drones to inject emergency medication into injured personnel at distant locations, buying time for treatment. Advances in unmanned technologies are making unmanned equipment an increasingly important part of aeromedical rescue, helping overcome the limitations of traditional rescue operations. Global Times

item.title: Is investigation into Jensen Huang about counter-espionage, or is it a political witch hunt?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 15:50:00
Jensen Huang. Photo: VCG One woman, one affair, and a national security narrative that the American media have spun with more imagination than evidence. That was all it took to thrust one of US' most powerful tech CEOs into the middle of a "spy" controversy. On Sunday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair - but whether this marks the end of the media storm or just the beginning remains to be seen. It started with an accusation from The New York Times. Beginning with its October 29 article and continuing in a series of follow-ups, the newspaper claimed that a woman who had held an executive role at a Singapore-based data center company was suspected of working for China's military and top spy agency. According to the reports, she had developed a "close relationship" with Huang and allegedly helped China obtain advanced AI chips subject to US export controls. Western media quickly jumped on the story. Suddenly, it had all the ingredients of a political spy thriller: Chinese intelligence agencies, cutting-edge AI chips, alleged corporate infiltration, an intimate personal relationship, and the head of one of the US' most vital tech companies. It's quite a story, complete with all the twists and suspense of a Hollywood thriller. But so far, the public has seen no hard evidence to back up the central allegations. The key claims in the media reports rely heavily on anonymous sources and materials that the media could not verify. China's Foreign Ministry rejected the allegations on October 30, calling relevant report unsubstantiated and nothing but smears against China. The ministry reiterated the statement on Monday. The Ministry of Home Affairs of Singapore has also rejected a Wall Street Journal report citing sources who said Singapore officials had concerns about, and had investigated, a businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. It stated that neither the Singapore Government nor its officials said this and there were no such investigations. Meanwhile, the political stakes in Washington keep rising. On Sunday, the NVIDIA Board announced an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. However, it also stressed that the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised. Additionally, three House chairmen want Huang to brief them privately on November 18. Who are these anonymous sources cited by the American media? Where is the hard, independently verifiable evidence? Why are these allegations surfacing now? And perhaps most importantly, who stands to benefit? For now, none of these questions has a clear answer. But one thing is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: Huang is no longer simply weathering a media storm over his private life; he is facing a controversy with unmistakable political overtones. The episode is beginning to follow a familiar pattern of political targeting: US media outlets amplify the claims allegedly supplied by insiders and frame them as a national security threat; politicians pile on; and before any investigation has reached its conclusions, the court of public opinion has already begun passing judgment. One fact should not be overlooked. In an environment where US competition with China is increasingly politicized, Chinese heritage can turn ordinary business ties into objects of political suspicion. Huang is a US citizen. The company he leads is a pillar of the US' AI strength. Yet he has been swept into a media storm over alleged Chinese intelligence activity. This raises a pointed question: when an American entrepreneur's business network intersects with China, is he seen first as an American entrepreneur - or first as an ethnic Chinese person who must face extra scrutiny? There is another backdrop that cannot be ignored: political infighting. Political divisions in the US over AI development are widening. The current administration is pushing hard on AI investment and data-center construction. Some Democrats, however, want to slow that expansion, citing concerns over energy use, environmental impact, and the power of tech giants. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has long pressed Huang to testify on Nvidia's China-related business and its approach to export controls. Those efforts were previously limited by procedural hurdles, including subpoena power. After Democrats regain control of both chambers of Congress, would the path to similar investigations and subpoenas become significantly smoother? A country's technological competitiveness ultimately rests on innovation, talent, and confidence in its own institutions. When the heads of the US' leading tech companies must, beyond normal commercial activity, continuously pass political loyalty tests that lack clear standards, it reveals a deeper anxiety in the US about the global AI race. Suspicion alone will not produce the next generation of GPUs. Over-politicizing scrutiny and the habit of framing business ties as security risks will not win the next round of AI competition. The truly strong are busy building what comes next. Only those growing more anxious go looking for enemies nearby.

item.title: 14 killed, 60 rescued in apartment fire in North China's Shanxi; property management personnel placed under control: local authorities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 11:33:00
Firefighters work to extinguish a blaze at a high-rise building in Yingze district, Taiyuan, North China's Shanxi Province, on November 8, 2026. Firefighting operations were still underway as of 7 pm. Photo: VCG A fire at an apartment building in Taiyuan, North China's Shanxi Province, has killed 14 people, while 60 others were evacuated or rescued, with management personnel of the property owner and personnel in charge of the property management company been placed under control measures, local authorities said at a press briefing on Monday afternoon, Xinhua reported. The briefing, held by the Publicity Department of the Taiyuan Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, provided an update on the fire at Haosheng International Apartment. The fire broke out at an apartment building in Yingze district, Taiyuan, at 4:59 pm on Sunday. The open flames were extinguished by 7 pm, and search and rescue operations concluded at 8:30 pm, CCTV News reported earlier. At around 7:30 pm on Sunday, firefighters were using high-altitude firefighting equipment to spray water on the fire-hit area near the top of the building to prevent the flames from reigniting, while smoke continued to billow from some floors, a reporter from China National Radio (CNR) reported from the scene. Flashlights could be seen moving behind the windows of the burned floors as rescue personnel searched for people inside. Signboards of several training institutions were visible on the building's exterior. Local residents told the reporter that the building housed several training institutions and was adjacent to a hotel. Following the incident, Taiyuan immediately activated its emergency response plan and set up a task force to oversee rescue and response efforts, with dedicated teams for medical treatment, post-accident arrangements, accident investigation and accountability, and overall coordination. The city has mobilized medical resources across the province and municipality to treat the injured, adopting an individual treatment plan and dedicated support team for each patient, according to the briefing. Authorities are also providing assistance to the families of those killed, offering emotional support to the injured and handling compensation matters. Management personnel of the property owner and personnel in charge of the property management company have been placed under control measures, the briefing said. In response to the accident, Taiyuan will conduct a citywide campaign to comprehensively inspect, identify and address workplace safety risks, with a particular focus on fire safety and high-risk industries, in a bid to prevent similar incidents and protect people's lives and property. Global Times
